paras: The attempted hanging of Andrew Holbrook took place in Newport News, Virginia, on the night of August 28, 1905, when grocer Frank L. Townsend and members of his household bound Holbrook, a Black man, and tied a rope around his neck. Spectators drawn by his cries persuaded Townsend to stop, and police took Holbrook away; he was later jailed for six months for trying to break into Townsend's lunch wagon. Wire versions of the story ran in papers as far away as Illinois and Kentucky under headlines such as "Negro Saved From Lynching."

Townsend kept a home and grocery store at 233 Thirty-third Street and drove a lunch wagon to the shipyard every day. Holbrook, who was said to work at the shipyard, was accused of attempting to break into that wagon in company with another Black man, Sam Barksdale.

Shortly after 10 o'clock that night, cries from the rear yard brought about half a dozen men running from Washington Avenue and the nearby Eagles' home. They found a Black man on the ground, bound hand and foot, with two women and a man in night clothes seated on him while Townsend, in a nightshirt, tied a half-inch rope around his neck. According to eyewitnesses, Townsend then threw the rope over a beam; his daughter fled into the house, while Mrs. Townsend sat on a box and, witnesses said, urged him to "Go ahead and hang him."

Several onlookers called on Townsend to stop, and voices from a neighboring house cried "Don't kill that man!" Townsend gave up the hanging but, the witnesses said, beat the man in the dirt and struck him over the head with a club. Someone telephoned for the patrol wagon, and Driver Pelham Smith and Patrolman Woodward untied the prisoner and took him to the station.

When Holbrook appeared in police court the next day, the Daily Press noted that the rope mark was plainly visible on his neck. Officer Padgett arrested Barksdale the same day, and Chief Reynolds at first believed both men were wanted in Danville for housebreaking. After Danville authorities wrote that their witnesses had scattered, the pair were tried locally, and Justice Brown gave each six months in jail. No report that Townsend was arrested or charged appears in the coverage.

The Newport News Daily Press gave the story a long, detailed treatment under the headline "Timely Interference Prevented F. L. Townsend From Hanging Alleged Negro Thief." Its account mixed alarm with ridicule: the scene was at first "ludicrous," Townsend was said to be playing "the part of Judge Lynch," and the victim was called a "much battered 'coon.'" Its first follow-up, headed "Both Are Old Offenders," stressed Holbrook's earlier prison term for shooting Barksdale.

A Newport News special to the Richmond Times-Dispatch and a wire version carried by the Alexandria Gazette condensed the episode, describing Holbrook as a man who "attempted to break into" the wagon and "narrowly escaped death at the hands of the grocer." The Washington Evening Star and the Shepherdstown Register ran the wire within days, and the Cairo Bulletin and Paducah Sun reprinted it on September 6.

The first Daily Press report named the victim Andrew Holman, but the same paper's later stories and the wire called him Andrew Holbrook. One wire reprint placed the attack on Tuesday rather than Monday night, the date given by the local paper the next morning.

reader.title: Attempted hanging of Andrew Holbrook
bases: A white grocer and members of his household bound a Black man accused of theft, tied a rope around his neck and threw it over a beam before bystanders intervened, which the local paper cast as playing "Judge Lynch" (A1, A3, A4).

Holbrook survived and was taken away by police (A1, A2), so no one was killed; the binding involved Townsend and three others in his yard, acting without authority on an accusation of theft (A1), which makes this an attempted lynching rather than a lynching.

The local Daily Press eyewitness account (A1), its police-court follow-up noting the rope mark (A2), and a separate Newport News special to the Richmond Times-Dispatch (A3) agree on the core event, though the outside reports may share a local source.

accounts.label: Eyewitnesses via the local Daily Press
accounts.gist: Spectators found the man bound under four figures in night clothes, saw Townsend throw the rope over a beam, heard Mrs. Townsend urge a hanging, and persuaded Townsend to stop; he then beat and clubbed the man.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A grocer whose lunch wagon a Black man tried to break into had a rope around the man's neck and was about to string him up when people drawn by the cries interfered; the wife's remark is reported as alleged.

framing.detail: The Daily Press headed it 'Timely Interference Prevented F. L. Townsend From Hanging Alleged Negro Thief', called the scene at first 'ludicrous' and Townsend's act a 'wild performance', while calling the victim a 'coon' and an 'old offender'.

Outside papers ran the wire under headings such as 'Attempt to Hang Negro', 'Negro Saved From Lynching' and 'Would Hang Negro Himself', describing the man as one 'who attempted to break into' the wagon.

conflicts.note: Only the first, truncated report uses Holman; the same paper's three follow-ups and the wire use Holbrook, the better-attested form.
The local paper, published the next morning, is the better evidence; one wire reprint gives Tuesday.
